title: Reading Errors, Asking Useful Debugging Questions and Saving Versions
learningObjectives: Explain the main ideas in your own words
Apply the workflow to a small project
Identify mistakes and correct them safely

understand.concept: An error is information about something that did not work as expected. Syntax errors break language rules, runtime errors happen while code runs, and logic errors produce the wrong result even though the program runs.
understand.whyItMatters: Debug systematically: reproduce the problem, read the first useful error message, note the file and line, inspect the nearby code, change one thing at a time, then test again. A useful question includes what you expected, what happened, the smallest relevant code and the exact error text.
understand.history: This lesson focuses on current, practical web-development concepts; historical claims are omitted where they are not needed.
understand.analogy: Debugging is like tracing a fault in a machine by checking one component at a time. The analogy has limits: software behaviour can depend on state, timing, environment and inputs, so record the conditions that reproduce the issue. Save named versions or use version control so a working state can be restored.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only a learning aid, not a complete description of technical behaviour.
